sections.h2: Which offices tax a Cincinnati house?
sections.html:
Cincinnati is both the largest city in Hamilton County and its seat, and county offices run the whole property tax process. The Hamilton County Auditor assigns each parcel a market value. The Hamilton County Treasurer sends the bills and collects payment at 138 East Court Street, Room 402, reachable at 513-946-4800 on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m.

Value disputes go to the county Board of Revision. The treasurer's real estate page says three officials sit on it: the county auditor, the county treasurer and the president of the board of county commissioners. The city of Cincinnati levies and receives its share, but it neither values nor bills your house.

sections.h2: When were the 2026 Cincinnati property tax bills due?
sections.html:
The treasurer's home page lists first-half bills mailed January 16, 2026 and due February 10, 2026. Second-half bills were mailed July 2 and fell due July 24, 2026. That second date was a late change. A June 22, 2026 press release said state legislation requiring an Inflation Cap Credit forced a recalculation of the second-half bills, which pushed the schedule back.

  • The county's pages say real estate taxes are paid twice a year, and the exact day is printed on each bill.
  • A payment up to ten days late carries a 5 percent penalty. After that the penalty rises to 10 percent.
  • The treasurer's site offers a Penalty Remit Application for owners who want to request relief.
  • There is no discount for paying early, though a prepayment program called TOP lets owners pay ahead in installments.

Future years may land on different dates, so check the bill and the treasurer's site each cycle.

sections.h2: How do you pay a Cincinnati property tax bill?
sections.html:
The office accepts payment four ways, according to its payment page.

  • Online through Point & Pay, with a $1.00 fee for an eCheck or 2.35 percent for a credit card. The county does not keep those fees.
  • By phone through Point & Pay at 1-877-764-3524.
  • By mail, with a personal check, cashier's check or money order payable to Hamilton County Treasurer. Write the bill stub or parcel number on the memo line.
  • In person at 138 E. Court St., Room 402. Cash is accepted only at the counter.

A mailed payment counts as on time if it is postmarked on or before the due date. The page warns that the Postal Service now postmarks mail when it goes through a sorting machine, which can be later than the day you dropped it in a box. Near a deadline, ask a post office clerk to stamp the envelope by hand.

sections.h2: How is a Cincinnati tax bill built from levies?
sections.html:
The treasurer's glossary explains the steps. Ohio taxes only 35 percent of a parcel's market value, a figure called assessed value. A mill is $1 for each $1,000 of assessed value, and rates are quoted in mills. A reduction factor holds voted levies to the revenue they were approved to raise, so reappraisals do not automatically lift them. The state then applies credits, including a non-business credit on residential property, an owner occupancy credit and the homestead credit.

The same page lists the countywide levies that show on a Cincinnati bill. School district, township and city levies are separate lines on the bill. The page also notes that every Hamilton County district except Cincinnati and Northwest pays the Great Oaks career campus levy.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Cincinnati property value?
sections.html:
A complaint goes to the Hamilton County Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31. The treasurer's page repeats that window and points to the Board of Revision website for forms and instructions, and its FAQ lists 513-946-4035 as the board's phone number. Section 5715.19 backs the deadline: March 31 of the year after the tax year, or the end of first-half collection if later. A postmark by that day counts for mailed filings.

The market value is the part you can contest, because tax levies are set by voters and local governments. The treasurer's FAQ says the amount of tax depends on both and that only the value can be challenged. While a complaint is pending, an owner may tender tax computed on the value claimed in it.

sections.h2: What can a Cincinnati owner do about delinquent taxes?
sections.html:
The treasurer's delinquent taxes page sets out the ladder. Interest and penalties start at once, and a taxpayer who is behind can ask for a delinquent contract at 513-946-4800. A contract in good standing protects the property from further penalties, interest, tax foreclosure and a lien sale.

  • Taxes still unpaid after the second-half collection period are certified delinquent in November and become eligible for a tax lien sale in October of the next year, usually around the second week of the month.
  • The county sells eligible liens as a block to financial institutions and does not sell individual lien certificates. Once a lien is sold, added fees attach to the property.
  • A tax foreclosure is a court case filed by the county prosecutor. The owner usually has 28 days to answer the summons, and a judgment leads to a sheriff's sale held online.

One program was aimed at Cincinnati owners. A county announcement dated August 18, 2025 described a one-time effort, funded by the city with help from the Landbank and a nonprofit counselor, to retire delinquent liens on about 250 homes before the 2025 bills came due in 2026. Eligible homes were owner-occupied one or two family houses worth $100,000 or less, with $10,000 or less owed as of July 2025, and eligible owners were notified by mail.

sections.h2: Does Cincinnati offer homestead or other tax credits?
sections.html:
The state homestead exemption applies in Cincinnati like anywhere else in Ohio. The Department of Taxation says that for tax year 2026 it equals the tax on $29,700 of value for low-income seniors and disabled owners, with a $41,000 income limit, and $59,400 for disabled veterans with no income test. Applications go to the county auditor.

The treasurer's FAQ also says the stadium sales tax credit appears automatically when an owner receives the 2.5 percent owner occupancy rollback, which applies to a home you own and occupy. The state FAQ sets the filing deadline at December 31 of the year the credit is sought.

sections.h2: What should you know about Cincinnati itself before selling a house there?
sections.html:
Cincinnati sits on the Ohio River across from the Licking River's mouth in Kentucky, with downtown on flat land near the water and the rest of the city spread over hills and ridges. The city counts 52 neighborhoods. Over-the-Rhine, built largely by German immigrants between 1865 and the 1880s, is among the largest intact urban historic districts in the country, and Westwood has the most residents. Norwood, Elmwood Place and St. Bernard are enclaves inside the city limits and have their own governments, so check which jurisdiction a street belongs to. Since 1922 the official Ohio flood stage at Cincinnati has been 52 feet, and the river's record crest came in January 1937.

  • Population: 314,367 in July 2025, up 1.5 percent from the April 2020 base.
  • Owner-occupied share of homes, 2020 to 2024: 39.8 percent.
  • Midpoint value of an owner-occupied home: $230,900.
  • Median household income: $52,909, with 25.5 percent in poverty.
  • Median gross rent: $1,001, across 144,297 households.

Those numbers are from Census QuickFacts. With owners holding fewer than four in ten homes, many sellers here are landlords or heirs, who should confirm the tax status of every parcel they own.

sections.h2: How does a tax bill affect a fast sale in Cincinnati?
sections.html:
Taxes stay attached to the property, so a buyer's title search finds any unpaid half. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure, including prior years, and give it to the closing agent. If a lien has already been sold, the treasurer's office can tell you who holds it, and a payoff must include that holder's added fees.

Sellers who are behind on taxes but want to keep the house have a second path: sign a delinquent contract ahead of the lien sale, which keeps the property out of it as long as current taxes stay paid.

faqs.q: What number reaches the office that sends Cincinnati tax bills?
faqs.a: The Hamilton County Treasurer answers at 513-946-4800 on weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., from Room 402 at 138 East Court Street. The FAQ gives 513-946-4035 for Board of Revision questions about value.

faqs.q: When was the second half of the 2026 Cincinnati tax due?
faqs.a: July 24, 2026. Bills were mailed July 2. The date was moved from the usual schedule because state law required an Inflation Cap Credit to be built into the second-half bills.

faqs.q: What penalty applies to a late Cincinnati property tax payment?
faqs.a: The penalty is 5 percent for the first 10 days after the due date and 10 percent after that, according to the treasurer's real estate page. The same page offers a Penalty Remit Application.

faqs.q: When can I file a Cincinnati property value complaint?
faqs.a: From January 1 through March 31. They go to the Hamilton County Board of Revision, and a mailed filing is timely when its postmark carries a date of March 31 or earlier.

faqs.q: Can the county sell my Cincinnati house for unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Only through foreclosure. A tax lien sale transfers the lien, not the house, and after a year the lien holder may start foreclosure. A delinquent contract entered before the sale, with current taxes kept paid, keeps the property off the lien list.
